*   **Key points:** • A new multiple-scale 3-D shear wave velocity model of the southern segment of the Tanlu Fault Zone was constructed based on a dense seismic array deployed in Hefei and Chao Lake.  • Our new model indicates significant low velocity anomalies in Hefei City, which helps further research on urban ground motion simulation adjacent to the large active fault zone.  • Strong ground motion during the _M_ 3.5 Feidong earthquake in 2019 may be related to the urban sedimentary environment.
Regional high-precision velocity models of the crust are an important foundation for examining seismic activity, seismogenic environments, and disaster distribution characteristics.
The Hefei-Chao Lake area contains the main geological units of Hefei Basin, with thick sediments and the Chao Lake depression.
Several major concealed faults of the southern NNE-trending Tanlu Fault Zone cross this area.

To further explore the underground distribution characteristics of the faults and their tectonic evolutionary relationship with adjacent tectonic units, this study used ambient noise data recorded by a seismic array deployed in Hefei City and Chao Lake, constructing a 3-D velocity model at the depth of 1–8 km.
Then a multi-scale high-resolution 3-D velocity model of this area was constructed by this new upper crustal velocity model with the previous middle and lower crustal model.

The new model reveals that a high-velocity belt is highly consistent with the strike of the Tanlu Fault Zone, and a low-velocity sedimentary characteristic is consistent with the Hefei Basin and Chao Lake depression.

The distribution morphology of high and low velocity bodies shows that the sedimentary pattern of Hefei-Chao Lake area is closely related to the tectonic evolution of the Tanlu Fault Zone since the Mesozoic.
This study also identifies multiple low-velocity anomalies in the southeastern Hefei City.
We speculate that strong ground motion during the 2009 Feidong earthquake (magnitude of 3.5) was related to amplification by the thick sediments in the Hefei Basin.
We also discuss further applications of multi-scale high-resolution models of the shallow layer to strong ground motion simulations in cities and for earthquake disaster assessments.
The Hefei-Chao Lake area is located in the mid-east of the Chinese mainland.
The Tanlu Fault crosses the Hefei area and Chao Lake, the fifth largest freshwater lake in China.
The Tanlu Fault Zone is a giant fault zone that remains active in the eastern Chinese mainland.
The middle-south segment of the fault zone spans three provinces: Jiangsu, Shandong, and Anhui.
The southern part extends to Lujiang County in Anhui Province and borders the Dabie orogenic belt.
It forms the tectonic boundary between the North China block and the South China block.
Different tectonic units and multiple structures of the extensional basin are distributed on both sides of Tanlu Fault Zone.
Historically, a strong earthquake (magnitude of 8.5) occurred in Tancheng, Shandong, as well as many events of magnitudes ≥ 5.
Most of the earthquakes of magnitudes ≥ 4 in Anhui Province have occurred on the west side of the Tanlu Fault Zone and its adjacent area.
Different from the central and northern segments, the southward extension of the Tanlu Fault Zone breaks up gradually, and the major faults of most branches are concealed throughout Anhui Province.
Therefore, knowledge of possible seismogenic structures in this area is limited.
Hefei City is located on the southeastern edge of the Hefei Basin.

Geological studies have shown that the tectonic evolution and sedimentary patterns in Hefei Basin since the Mesozoic are closely related to activity along the Tanlu Fault Zone (Liu GS et al., 2002; Zhu G et al., 2001).

Although seismic activity in Hefei Basin is not significant, the 1673 Hefei earthquake (magnitude of 5.0) occurred at the center of Hefei City and the 1585 earthquake (magnitude of 5.75) occurred on the south bank of Chao Lake.
In 2009, a magnitude 3.5 earthquake occurred in Feidong County, which is in the interior of the Tanlu Fault Zone and 20 km away from Hefei City.
Although the magnitude of this earthquake was not large, the ground motion and impact on the social life in the city were substantial.

Studies have shown that low-velocity sedimentary layers can amplify seismic signals, thereby increasing the destructiveness of earthquakes (Bonilla et al., 1997; Maufroy et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2016; Chamlagain and Gautam, 2015).
Therefore, the risk of earthquake disasters in cities overlying sedimentary basins cannot be ignored.
There are two main methods for performing earthquake disaster assessments.
The first is observations of strong ground motion based on strong earthquakes (Hartzell and Heaton, 1983; Bradley et al., 2017; Takai et al., 2016; Zhang W et al., 2008; Zhang L et al., 2016).
The second is ground motion simulation based on 3-D velocity models (Lee et al., 2007; Chaljub et al., 2015; Boore, 2003).

There is no record of strong earthquakes of magnitudes ≥ 6 in Hefei City and adjacent areas, such that the method of observing strong ground motion based on strong earthquakes is not applicable in this area.
Instead, 3-D velocity models and ground motion simulations can be used to effectively assess potential earthquake disasters.
Therefore, this method is suitable for investigating cities where the seismic activity is weak, but disaster risks are high.
However, a reliable urban ground motion simulation must be based on high-precision models of the shallow crust to accurately assess earthquake disaster risks.
At present, there is no unified fine velocity model for Hefei and its adjacent areas.
Most existing velocity models in the surrounding areas have been constructed at the tectonic block scale (Luo S et al., 2019; Li HY et al., 2018), with a lateral resolution of 0.5°–1°.
Their applications to the analysis of small-scale fine structures are limited.
In terms of the depths used in previous studies, few studies have been conducted on the fine structures at a few kilometers or only 1 km below the fault.

Observations from existing dense survey lines across the Tanlu Fault Zone in northern Hefei can achieve a high resolution (Qin JJ et al., 2018), but the understanding of the 3-D fault structure is still limited.
The Southern California Community Velocity Model (CVM) is a typical community velocity model (Lee et al., 2014; Shaw et al., 2015).
This high-resolution and high-precision CVM provides an important foundation for seismological research in the Southern California.

In 2016, the China Seismic Experimental Site began to systematically construct community velocity models in the Sichuan-Yunnan area at four different scales, i.e., the regional block scale, the fault zone scale, the fault scale, and the urban scale, with lateral resolutions of 10–50, 1–5, 0.1–0.5, and about 1 km, respectively.
This project has thus far made preliminary progress (Yao HJ, 2020; Liu Y et al., 2021).
The integration of high-precision models at different scales can provide an important foundation for regional seismology research.

Luo S et al. (2019) used data from 107 permanent stations and 82 temporary stations in eastern China to invert for the crustal velocity model of the southern segment of the Tanlu Fault Zone and the middle and lower Yangtze River, with a lateral resolution of 30–50 km.

This is significant for understanding the distribution of the main tectonic units and the differences in fault properties, structural characteristics, and mantle dynamics; it also provides an important foundation for establishing multi-scale fine velocity models.
Recently, ambient noise tomography based on short-period dense seismic arrays has been rapidly applied to investigate velocity structures in the shallow crust.
This technology has provided significant advantages in terms of model construction at the urban scale and the fault zone scale.
Li C et al. (2016) used 17 short-period stations inside the Hefei first ring road to obtain the velocity model of Hefei City within 400 m below Earth’s surface.
Li C et al. (2020) used 58 short-period temporary stations in Hefei City to record ambient noise and invert for the shear wave velocity model at a depth of approximately 4 km.
Luo S and Yao HJ (2021) used data from 117 stations deployed around Chao Lake to obtain a 3-D velocity model within a depth of 10 km.
Additionally, small-scale short-period arrays have been recently used to reveal shallow crustal structures in Feidong and Lujiang area (Gu N et al., 2019; Li C et al., 2020).

Based on the studies mentioned above, we combined data from the short-period arrays in Hefei City, Chao Lake, and Feidong to invert for the shallow crustal velocity model of the Hefei area (including three counties, one city, and the water area of Chao Lake), which includes a total of four branch faults along the eastern and western sides of the Tanlu Fault Zone.
Based on this shallow model, a multi-scale velocity model was constructed by the existing regional block-scale model.

The new model reveals the fault distribution morphology and deep structural characteristics beneath the southern segment of the Tanlu Fault Zone, with a high resolution (lateral resolution of 3–5 km) in the shallow crust to a regional scale (lateral resolution up to 30 km) in the deep crust.
This model provides an important foundation for investigating the seismic activity, strong ground motion, and disaster assessments in the Hefei area.

In this study we used the short-period dense seismic arrays deployed in Hefei City, Feidong, and Chao Lake to collect vertical component data for approximately one month and extract the phase velocity dispersion curves of the noise surface waves with a period of 0.5–8.5 s.
Figure 1 shows the distribution of the arrays in the Hefei area, which is composed of three sub-arrays with 228 short-period seismometers in total.
The three sub-arrays are the Hefei City array, the Chao Lake array, and the Feidong array.

Among them, the Hefei City array and Chao Lake array were deployed during the same period (from September 30 to November 5, 2018) by the Anhui Earthquake Agency and the University of Science and Technology of China, respectively.
The array in the Feidong area was deployed by the University of Science and Technology of China in 2017.
All of the seismographs deployed at the stations were three-component short-period seismographs (model: QS-5A).
The sampling rate was 100 Hz and the recording time was approximately one month.
First, cross-correlation calculations were performed on the continuous waveform data from the vertical component from the Hefei City and Chao Lake sub-arrays for approximately 30 d (Figure 2).
The cross-correlation functions of all the station pairs were obtained.

Second, by utilizing the image analysis technique (Yao HJ et al., 2006, 2011) more than 12,000 phase velocity dispersion curves of the fundamental-mode Rayleigh wave, with a period band of 0.5–9 s, were extracted from the cross-correlation functions.
After strict quality control, more than 6,700 phase velocity curves were screened out.
The dispersion data of the Feidong sub-array were extracted in a previous study (Gu N et al., 2019).

Combined with the existing 0.2–5 s phase velocity dispersion data from the Feidong array, the phase velocity dispersion data, with a period band of 0.5–8.5 s (Figure 3), were used for subsequent inversion.
The direct inversion method based on surface wave travel times (Fang HJ et al., 2015) was employed to obtain the 3-D S-wave velocity model of the region.
The initial model used in the inversion was the regional average 1-D velocity model obtained from the average dispersion.
The grid setting in the east-west and south-north directions was both 0.02°.
In the depth direction, 19 layers were set, separated by 0.5 km between 0 and 4 km, 1 km between 4 and 10 km, and 2 km between 11 and 20 km.
Checkerboard tests were used for resolution analysis.
The size of the checkerboard anomaly was set as 0.04° for both directions.
Figure 4 shows the recovery conditions at a depth of 1–8 km with overall good resolution.
After a total of five inversion iterations, the travel time residual value and its standard deviation were both reduced and remained stable (Figure 5).
This indicates that the inversion model was significantly improved compared to the initial model.
Figure 6 shows the horizontal sections of the 3-D S-wave velocity model at depths of 1–8 km; Figure 7 shows the final 1-D velocity models at different stations.
Based on the velocity models at different depths in Figure 6, there exist strong lateral heterogeneities in the study area.
Stations in uplift areas exhibit high velocities, whereas depression areas show low velocities (Figures 7a and 7b).
To the east of Hefei City and across Chao Lake, perpendicular to the Tanlu Fault Zone, the velocity structure shows a step-like change between high and low velocities.
Hefei City and the eastern half of Chao Lake in the eastern Hefei basin show notable anomalies with low velocities.
These anomalies are separated by NNE band-like anomalies with high velocities, which are consistent with the directions of the east branch fault along the Tanlu Fault Zone and at Yinping mountain.
This type of step-like velocity change is consistent with the known geological structure characteristics.
In Hefei City, the Wuhe-Hefei fault on the west branch of the Tanlu Fault Zone and the Chihe-Xishanyi fault along the east branch notably control the sedimentary pattern of the Feidong depression.

The depth of the low-velocity center reaches to approximately 6 km, which is consistent with the position of the sedimentary zone between Huangli and Wangji in the Feidong area based on deep seismic reflection (Qin JJ et al., 2018).
This shows that the Tanlu Fault Zone controls the sedimentary pattern in the eastern Hefei Basin.
Under the waters of Chao Lake, the major east branch fault along the Tanlu Fault Zone separates the lake into eastern and western parts.
The eastern part presents a large area of low velocity, which is strip-like distributed in the same direction as the fault zone.
It is blocked by the uplift of Yinping Mountain to the east and has a center of low velocity at a depth of approximately 6 km.
Additionally, the velocity cross-sections at different depths show a distinct boundary between the high and low velocities in the Hefei basin at approximately 31.4° N with a ENE strike direction.
This area borders the northern edge of Dabie Mountain and Hefei basin, which is characterized by the intersection of multiple groups of faults.
Many fractured zones also exist at the surface, which are possibly related to the eastward extension of the WNW fault.

The velocity model of the crust (5–40 km) along the middle and lower Yangtze River reported in Luo S et al. (2019) was also collected for integration with the shallow crustal model (0–8 km) proposed in this study.
After weighted average of the model data at their common depths (5–8 km), a final velocity model of different scales from the shallow crust to the deep crust was constructed (Figure 8).
The Hefei-Chao Lake area is at the southern end of the Tanlu Fault Zone and adjacent to the northern edge of the Dabie Mountains.
The southern segment of the Tanlu Fault Zone shows a tectonic pattern of “two grabens on the sides and one horst in the middle” in Shandong and northern Jiangsu, but this pattern disappears in Anhui.
At the same time, the major fault along the Tanlu Fault Zone gradually disappears within the Quaternary rocks of the Hefei Basin.
Therefore, our understanding of the geometric distribution morphology of this segment in Anhui is insufficient, especially the tectonic characteristics of the shallow surface.

Recent results based on shallow ambient noise tomography near Hefei show that the high-velocity anomalies adjacent to the Tanlu Fault Zone contrast significantly with the low-velocity anomalies inside the sedimentary area (Gu N et al., 2019; Li LL et al., 2020; Li C et al., 2020).

Based on our results (Figure 6), the geometric distribution morphology of the four major faults in the Tanlu Fault Zone, especially the shear wave velocity in the direction perpendicular to the fault zone, presents a notable step-like jump, which is consistent with the known tectonics of the surface.
Deep and large fault zones are often the main controlling factors of sedimentation in basins.
Our results show that the morphology of the low-velocity area in the Hefei area coincide with the sedimentary morphology of the southeastern Hefei Basin and the eastern depression at Chao Lake.
The Tanlu Fault Zone, as a deep and large fault that cuts through the crust, has a notable control over the basins and depressions on both sides within these areas.
This is closely related to the multi-phase tectonic activity of the fault since the Mesozoic and Cenozoic.
The _A_-_A_’, _B_-_B_’, and _E_-_E_’ cross-sections, perpendicular to the Tanlu Fault Zone, also reveal the lateral changes in the structure on both sides of this zone (Figure 9).
Section _A_-_A_’ traverses Feidong depression, where the depth of the low-velocity sedimentary area on the eastern side of the Tanlu Fault Zone reaches to approximately 5 km.
The velocity is especially low at depths > 2 km.

The bedrock geological map of this area shows that the sedimentary depth since the Cretaceous is approximately 1.5–2 km in the Feidong depression (Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources of Anhui Province, 1978).
This is consistent with the distribution of the low-velocity anomalies obtained in this study.
The Tanlu Fault Zone has many branch faults.

Based on our results, the Wuhe-Hefei fault along the western branch and the Chihe-Xishanyi fault along the eastern branch are the main basin-controlling faults and main influencing factors on the sedimentary patterns of the Feidong depression.

The Meishan-Longhekou fault in southwestern Hefei and the northern edge of the Dabie Mountains is usually considered as the southern boundary of the Hefei Basin (Dai Y et al., 2011), but the Xinyang-Shucheng fault is also considered as the southern boundary by some other studies (Liu GS et al., 2006).
However, the difference between these two faults, especially along eastern segments, remains unclear.
Some studies suggest that the Xinyang-Shucheng and Meishan-Longhekou faults, which extend to the eastern edge of the Dabie Mountains, may have different branches.
These faults are referred to as the Meishan-Longhekou fault in Anhui.
No branch faults were found at the surface during the geological and geomorphological survey near Shucheng.
Moreover, neither the Meishan-Longhekou fault nor the Xinyang-Shucheng fault shows a tendency to extend eastward to the Tanlu Fault Zone.

The boundary belts between the high and low velocities to the ENE appear on both sides of 31.4° N at different depths (Figure 6), which is different from the known strike and location of the Meishan-Longhekou fault; it is near the Xinyang-Shucheng fault, but with a different direction.

We speculate that this is an eastward extension of the Xinyang-Shucheng fault, which is intercepted by the Tanlu Fault Zone to the east, forming the southern boundary of Hefei Basin along the front of the Dabie Mountains.
Chao Lake is the fifth largest freshwater lake in China.
The Tanlu Fault Zone in a northeastern direction divides it into eastern and western areas.
The geological/geomorphology features around Chao Lake were caused by complex crustal evolution in Yanshan period in the Mesozoic and Himalayan period in the Cenozoic.

Short-period dense array tomography around Chao Lake has revealed, for the first time, that the velocity structure across the eastern branch of the Tanlu Fault Zone shows a notable alternating pattern between high and low velocities (Luo S and Yao HJ, 2021); the anisotropy characteristics of the upper crust show that the tectonic deformation of the Chao Lake area is closely related to the tectonic activities of the Tanlu Fault Zone during different periods (Luo S et al., 2021).
The B-B’ and E-E’ cross-sections show signs of westward compression of a high-velocity body beneath Yinping Mountain (shown in red boxes in Figure 9).
Geological studies suggest that Yinping Mountain is characterized by westward nappe tectonics.
Luo S et al. (2019) suggest that the morphology of the low-velocity body in the eastern half of Chao Lake is related to the eastward compression of the Tanlu Fault Zone.
Our results indicate that this body may have also been simultaneously compressed westward by Yinping Mountain.
In our new model, there are several significant low-velocity areas in southeastern Hefei City.
The range extends to the northwestern edge of Chao Lake (Figure 10).
We performed several observations on these sections.
The No. 4 cross-section line traverses Cuo town, Feidong county.
Cuo town is the sedimentary center of the Feidong depression with a sedimentary depth of 2–3 km since the Cretaceous.
The velocity in the central area of Hefei city is < 2 km/s at a depth of < 4 km, significantly lower than its surroundings, which is consistent with the shape of the sedimentary layer in this area.
At depths 6–7 km the velocity is still lower, which may indicate that the Jurassic basement in this area has reached this depth.
Besides Cuo town in Feidong, another low-velocity area is in the Binhu New District in southeastern Hefei adjacent to Chao Lake (the No. 3 cross-section).
The low-velocity anomaly center in this area extends to approximately 2 km.
Another low-velocity area is in the Shucheng-Sanhe area in southern Hefei (the No. 2 cross-section).
This area is near the front of the Dabie Mountains and has a notable jump at the mountain front fault near 31.4°–31.5°.
This mountain front fault is close to the Meishan-Longhekou fault.
The No.2 cross-section shows that this boundary fault is in a southeastern direction and may be the southern edge of the Hefei Basin.

Figure 11 shows the 3-D low-velocity characteristics at the shallow surface in the Hefei-Chao Lake area, which reveals that Hefei City is located at the sedimentary center in the southeastern Hefei Basin, and has a wide range of low S-wave velocities in the shallow crust and at the surface.

Disasters caused by many major earthquakes show that basins can significantly amplify long-period ground motion and increase the duration of ground motion, thereby causing serious damage to the urban structure.

A series of destructive earthquakes have verified that surface sedimentation is one of the main factors affecting seismic vibrations, such as in the 1985 Mexico earthquake and the 1999 Chi-Chi earthquake (Dalguer et al., 2001; Sanchez, 1989).
In 2015, an earthquake (magnitude of 4.3) in Fuyang, Anhui, occurred on the Hehuai Plain in North China; its magnitude was not large, but it still caused severe casualties.
Hong DQ et al. (2017) calculated that the focal depth of this earthquake was shallow (~3 km), suggesting that it may have occurred within the sedimentary layer, which caused substantial damage.
Hefei Basin is adjacent to the Tanlu Fault Zone and historically has a low seismic activity.
The only recorded earthquake of magnitude 5 (in 1673) occurred where the city is now located.
However, owing to a lack of historical seismic records, no detailed damage was recorded.
In 2009 an earthquake of magnitude 3.5 occurred at Liangyuan in Feidong, which is on the Tanlu Fault Zone and approximately 20 km from Hefei City (located along the No. 4 cross-section).
This earthquake had a small magnitude, but caused significant ground motion, which triggered a strong reaction from the inhabitants of Hefei City.

The low-velocity sedimentary structure in the Hefei Basin is a main influencing factor on ground motion in Hefei City, which may be the main reason for the occurrence of significant ground motion during the 2009 Feidong earthquake.
In densely populated large cities, especially those along fault zones with a strong earthquake potential, it is very important to focus more on the earthquake disasters.

Exploring the fault distribution in an urban area, obtaining 3-D fine structure models of the shallow surface, and simulating strong ground motion are particularly important to urban planning and seismic fortification.

However, in areas with low seismic activities, owing to a lack of observational data on ground motion from seismic instruments, obtaining comprehensive information on underground media and the site responses required for disaster assessment is difficult.

The U.S. Geological Survey carried out an online survey to collect high-frequency ground motion information, attempting to supplement the lack of ground motion data by collecting the responses to earthquakes from inhabitants in various parts of the United States (Atkinson and Wald, 2007).
From the perspective of a geophysical structure inversion, a reliable simulation of high frequency (> 1 Hz) ground motion requires a high-resolution (kilometer-level) velocity model.
Therefore, the construction of a high-resolution 3-D model is necessary.
Establishing a regional dense observation network is an effective means to improve the resolution.
However, the large-scale deployment of fixed or mobile arrays is not always feasible.
Local anomalies can also be easily ignored during large-scale anomaly analysis.
Yao HJ (2020) suggested to establish structural models at four different scales in response to the research requirements associated with the deep crustal structure of the Chinese mainland.
Models at a regional scale can provide a reference for solving scientific problems, such as the large-scale tectonic movement, deep Earth dynamics, and seismogenic environment.

Models at the fault zone scale, fault scale, and urban scale can provide necessary model foundations for investigating the seismogenic structures of faults and physical properties of structures adjacent to faults, as well as exploring physical models of the sources of strong earthquakes.

The integration of high-precision and high-resolution models at different scales can provide an important foundation for regional seismological research, especially providing reliable models for the middle and upper crust, or structural information on the seismogenic layer.
For model construction of the shallow surface and simulations of strong ground motion, multi-scale models must often consider the amplification of basins.
Many studies have adopted basin models based on drilling data as the basic reference for velocity models (Goto et al., 2005; Iwaki and Iwata, 2008).

Studies in China have also used geological sections and the structure of the sedimentary layer and crust obtained by artificial sources to simulate the wave-field propagation process and the distribution characteristics of strong ground motion for the 2008 Qinghai earthquake (magnitude of 6.3) (Chen YY et al., 2019).
However, more than one model exists for depths < 10 km.
Therefore, areas without survey lines have adopted the Crust1.0 model (Laske et al., 2013).
Furthermore, historical ground motion simulations at a small scale in cities require high-resolution and high-precision 3-D velocity structure models.

For urban areas with weak historical seismic activities, the predefined earthquake simulation using high-resolution shallow models can be used to obtain potential strong ground motion and provide approximate disaster information.
The model developed in this study has a high-resolution shallow crust, but the velocity model with depths < 1 km, especially shallower than 200–300 m depth, may be inaccurate.
This is primarily due to the lack of data of high-frequency surface wave dispersion.
Li C et al. (2016) constructed a shallow surface velocity model within the first ring road of Hefei City, constrained with well logging data in shallow depths.
For structures at 50 and 200 m depths (Figure 12), they observed the distinct change in the velocity structure across the Shushan Fault Zone near the surface.
Compared with the model in this study, the model proposed in Li C et al. (2016) has a significantly higher resolution and accuracy for the shallow layer.
Therefore, the establishment of a high-resolution urban-scale model and a reliable near-surface velocity model is the next step in the construction of a multi-scale model.

In this study, a new high-resolution and high-precision shear wave velocity model (0–8 km) of the upper crust was constructed from ambient noise tomography based on the dense seismic arrays deployed in Hefei-Chao Lake areas.
Our new model indicates strong lateral heterogeneities in study areas.
Significant low velocity anomalies exist in the southeastern Hefei City and the eastern part of Chao Lake, which is consistent with the tectonic features in the Hefei Basin and Chao Lake depression.

Our results suggest that low-velocity part in the eastern part of Chao Lake is related to the eastward compression of the Tanlu Fault Zone, and westward compression by Yinping Mountain, simultaneously.

The low-velocity sedimentary structure in the Hefei Basin is a main influencing factor on ground motion in Hefei City, which may be the reason for the occurrence of significant ground motion during the 2009 Feidong earthquake.
Based on the shallow crust model, we collected the previous lower resolution regional crustal model (5–40 km, by Luo S et al., 2019) for integration of the multi-scale crustal model (0–40 km).

The integration of high-precision and high-resolution models at different scales can provide an important foundation for regional seismological research, especially providing reliable models for the upper and middle crust, or structural information on the seismogenic layer.

In future work, we need to improve the model with lateral resolution of a kilometer level in the shallow upper crust and consider a better integration strategy for building a multi-scale crustal model.
